Actual Article Body:
Oct 22nd 2026

AI-generated, human-reviewed.

Meta Muse, the AI assistant launched by Meta, rapidly gained popularity for its convenience and deep integration. But recent discoveries show that its share chat feature left sensitive personal and business data exposed to public search—and all it took was a simple DNS query. On Tech News Weekly, Mikah Sargent provided a detailed public service advisory explaining how these oversights happened, who is at risk, and what every tech user should understand before trusting intelligent digital assistants with their private information.

The main vulnerability surfaced when security firm Clarock discovered that chat conversations shared using Meta Muse’s “share” button weren’t as private as users assumed. Typically, share links are designed with long random strings to keep content secure, accessible only to individuals who receive the direct link. However, with Muse, critical details—such as the title of a business conversation—were embedded in the subdomain of the URL.

This design decision meant that each time someone created a public link using Muse, it got logged by passive DNS systems. These systems maintain databases of past DNS queries, making it possible for anyone to search and list thousands of links containing descriptive chat titles like “loan-application-draft” or “q3-revenue-review.” As Mikah explained, this flaw made it trivially easy for security researchers to find over 6,800 share links, many containing highly sensitive data.

According to Mikah Sargent on Tech News Weekly, researchers reviewed a sample of these links and found:

Much of this information was never meant to be public. The risk wasn’t limited to potential hackers but included anyone who could search passive DNS databases and access functional share links—no special technical skills required.

After being alerted to the problem, Meta temporarily disabled the share chat function in Muse and acknowledged they were reviewing the issue. The company reiterated that privacy is a design priority, referencing its bug bounty program to identify and address problems. Yet, critics—including the security researchers involved—highlighted the gap between Meta’s privacy promises and the practical reality of how Muse’s features handled sensitive user information.

Importantly, this wasn’t the only security lapse with Muse since launch. A zero-day vulnerability allowing complete account takeover via another app on the same device was found just weeks prior, raising further concerns about the maturity and safety of Meta’s new AI platform.

On Tech News Weekly, Mikah Sargent advised listeners to exercise caution before granting deep account access to any AI-powered chatbot, not just Muse. Whenever users entrust passwords, financial info, or other sensitive data to digital assistants, a potential privacy or security slip can have wide consequences—not only due to direct hacking but also to accidental public exposure or company misconfiguration.

Users should:

Meta Muse’s security missteps serve as a cautionary tale: even services “designed for privacy” can suffer fundamental flaws that put user data at risk. Before handing over sensitive details to a digital assistant, consider the implications of potential leaks and stay informed about evolving security responses from vendors.
